newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: LAW UNCLEAR ON PURCHASE OF BALTIJOS MINORITY.
newsitem.headline: LAW UNCLEAR ON PURCHASE OF BALTIJOS MINORITY.

text.p: Brokers and officials are awaiting a decision by Lithuania's securities commission on whether Denmark's Odense Shipyard will have to offer to buy the remaining shares of Baltic Shipyard .
Odense said last week it controlled about 90 percent of the formerly state-owned Baltic Shipyard after it picked up the government's 16 percent stake at an auction at the stock exchange.
Odense is a subsidiary of Danish energy and shipping group A.P. Moeller .

According to Lithuanian law, companies that buy more than 50 percent of a company's voting shares are required to offer to buy the remaining shares at a weighted average of what they paid for their shares.
"This is supposed to be executed according to rules passed by the securities commission," Virgilijus Poderys, chairman of Lithuania's securities commission, told Reuters.
"But there are no rules. That's the problem," he said.
Poderys said the securities commission had not finished the rules and expected them to be completed in two months.
But Poderys said he was unsure what effect they would have on companies like Odense, who bought their shares before the rules had been written.
Poderys said the commission was divided over the issue but that the commission decision could affect majority shareholders in other companies, although he did not say which.
"Some members (of the commission) feel Odense should have to make the offer, others don't," Poderys added.

"It's very interesting to me that the securities commission cannot answer this question," said Tomas Andrejauskas, a broker with Suprema. "They should answer the question yes or no...no one else can answer this question."
"This is purely about the protection of shareholder rights, and the rules are not prepared," Andrejauskas said.
According to the stock exchange, Odense bought 43.53 percent of Baltic Shipyard shares at 10 litas a share in April.
Odense increased its stake to 74 percent when it later bought all of Baltic's new share issue at 10 litas a share.
Last week, Odense ran its stake up to about 90 percent when it bought the state's 16 percent stake at 10.10 litas a share.
Baltic Shipyard shares traded at eight litas on Monday on the Vilnius bourse.

For Baltic Shipyard shareholders, the dilemma is whether to sell at today's eight litas or wait to see if the securities commission will require Odense to make what by all accounts would be a higher offer, Andrejauskas said.
"It's vital for current shareholders," Andrejauskas said. "They are unsure of the situation."
But others say that a securities commission decision to apply the new rules to Odense retroactively would hurt foreign interest in the sleepy stock exchange.
"From a legal point of view it would be totally illogical now," said Robertas Berzhinskas, a broker with Vilniaus Bank. "It's an absolutely stupid idea."
"I don't think they want to destroy the reliability of the market," Berzhinskas said.
-- Vilnius newsroom 370 2 22 35 18
